summary: Recommends that DNS resolvers and recursive servers automatically serve certain zones locally unless configured otherwise. It extends the practice from the IPv6 case in RFC 4193 to the in-addr.arpa zones for RFC 1918 private address space and other well-known zones, keeping pointless queries off the public Internet.

plainLanguage.summary: Some questions, like who lives at a made-up private address, have no real answer on the public internet. This tells name servers to answer those on the spot instead of bothering far-away servers.

subtitle: Resolvers should answer reverse lookups for private and special addresses themselves, instead of sending them to the public Internet.

tldr.problem: Queries for reverse DNS names of private and other special addresses leak onto the public Internet, loading the servers that handle those zones and the root servers.
tldr.mechanism: Iterative resolvers and recursive nameservers should, unless configured otherwise, answer for a list of zones themselves, typically as empty zones that return name errors.
tldr.outcome: The list became the initial contents of an IANA registry, and the recommendation is meant to keep the number of sacrificial servers from growing.

today: RFC 6303 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 163) and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The zone list it started lives on in the IANA registry, which the RFC says can be amended through IETF Review.

sections.title: Introduction and Motivation
sections.content:
RFC 6303 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 163). It says that all iterative resolvers and recursive nameservers SHOULD automatically serve certain DNS zones locally, unless intentionally configured otherwise. The zones include the IN-ADDR.ARPA zones for the address space allocated by RFC 1918 and the IP6.ARPA zones for locally assigned unique local IPv6 addresses from RFC 4193.

The reason is query leakage. The RFC says data shows that significant leakage of queries for these namespaces is occurring, despite instructions to restrict them. That forced the deployment of sacrificial nameservers to protect the parent nameservers of these zones (the AS112 project, RFC 6304 and RFC 6305).

A second problem comes from clients behind badly configured firewalls that let queries out but drop the responses. These put load on the root servers and create work for the root server operators, who must answer enquiries about why the root servers are 'attacking' those clients.
sections.plainLanguage: Lots of computers keep asking far-away servers questions that have no real answer. It is like everyone calling the library to ask about a book that does not exist. Answering at home saves the library from the noise.

sections.title: Effects on Sites Using RFC 1918 Addresses
sections.content:
For most sites using RFC 1918 addresses, the change has little or no detrimental effect. If the site has not populated its reverse tree, the only difference is that the name error responses are generated locally rather than remotely.

Sites that do populate the reverse tree usually have a local copy of the zones or forward queries to servers that do, so the recommendation is not relevant to them.

The biggest impact is on sites that use delegations for RFC 1918 addresses and have populated these zones. They must override the default configuration so resolution keeps working. The RFC notes that such sites are typically fully disconnected from the Internet and run their own root servers for a separate DNS tree.
sections.plainLanguage: Most homes and offices will not notice anything. Only places that run their own private phone book need to tell their server not to do the new thing.

sections.title: How a Resolver Serves These Zones
sections.content:
Unless configured otherwise, an iterative resolver returns an authoritative (AA=1) name error (RCODE=3) for queries inside the listed zones. The exception is queries for the zone name itself, which get SOA, NS or 'no data' answers as appropriate. A common way to do this is to serve empty zones containing only SOA and NS records.

An implementation MUST provide a way to disable the behaviour and SHOULD allow the choice zone by zone.

For empty zones, the RFC says one SHOULD NOT reuse the NS and SOA records used on the public Internet servers, because that makes it harder to detect leakage. It is RECOMMENDED that the NS record defaults to the name of the zone and the SOA MNAME defaults to the target of that single NS record. The SOA RNAME SHOULD default to nobody.invalid., and implementations SHOULD let operators set these values. No address records are needed for the nameserver.

The SOA is needed for negative caching of name errors (RFC 2308) and to point clients to the primary master for dynamic updates. The NS record is needed because some UPDATE (RFC 2136) clients use NS queries to find the zone; having no address records is expected to abort UPDATE processing in the client. Both TTL values SHOULD match, and the other SOA timers MAY be chosen arbitrarily because they do not control zone transfers.
sections.plainLanguage: Your server keeps a tiny pretend phone book with nothing in it. When someone asks about a private address, it checks the empty book and says 'no such name' on the spot.

sections.title: The Zones Covered
sections.content:
Section 4 lists the zones. All are reverse zones for permanently assigned address space, and they became the initial contents of the IANA registry.

  • RFC 1918 zones: 10.IN-ADDR.ARPA, 16.172.IN-ADDR.ARPA through 31.172.IN-ADDR.ARPA, and 168.192.IN-ADDR.ARPA.
  • RFC 5735 and RFC 5737 zones: the IPv4 'this' network, loopback, link local, TEST-NET-1, TEST-NET-2, TEST-NET-3 and broadcast.
  • IPv6: the unspecified (::) and loopback (::1) addresses, D.F.IP6.ARPA for locally assigned local addresses, the four link-local zones 8.E.F.IP6.ARPA through B.E.F.IP6.ARPA, and the example prefix zone 8.B.D.0.1.0.0.2.IP6.ARPA.

Serving an empty 127.IN-ADDR.ARPA is not meant to discourage providing a PTR record for 1.0.0.127.IN-ADDR.ARPA locally. A meaningful reverse mapping should exist, but its setup is out of scope; the recommendation only assumes no other coverage exists.
sections.plainLanguage: This is the list of addresses that only make sense inside one place, like 'my room' or 'this building', so nobody far away can answer questions about them.

sections.title: Zones Left Out
sections.content:
Some zones are deliberately not covered. IPv6 site-local addresses are deprecated and expected to correct themselves as implementations remove support, though sacrificial servers for C.E.F.IP6.ARPA through F.E.F.IP6.ARPA may still be needed in the short term.

For IPv6 non-locally assigned local addresses (L = 0 in RFC 4193), no decision had been made on whether the Regional Internet Registries would delegate that space. If not, C.F.IP6.ARPA would be added to the list.

IP6.INT was deprecated in RFC 4159 and its delegation removed in June 2006, and is not treated as a local zone. Names directly under the root, such as .local and .workgroup, are also ignored because much of that traffic needs a different strategy.
sections.plainLanguage: A few odd corners are left alone on purpose, because the answer is not clear yet or needs a different fix.

sections.title: The IANA Registry
sections.content:
IANA established a registry of zones that require this default behaviour, with the zones from Section 4 as its initial contents. Implementors are encouraged to check it periodically and update their software. It can be amended through 'IETF Review' (RFC 5226).

The RFC warns that once a zone is added it is effectively added permanently: once an address range starts being configured as a local zone in systems on the Internet, it will be impossible to reverse that. IANA should also coordinate with the RIRs so that, as DNSSEC is deployed in the reverse tree, delegations are made as described in the security section.
sections.plainLanguage: There is an official list kept up to date, and once something goes on it, it stays, so adding to it needs care.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
During initial deployment, especially where RFC 1918 addresses are used, some clients may unexpectedly receive a name error instead of a PTR record. That can cause service disruption until their recursive nameservers are reconfigured.

As DNSSEC is deployed in IN-ADDR.ARPA and IP6.ARPA, the listed zones must be delegated as insecure delegations, or sit within insecure zones, so validation succeeds even though answers do not come from the delegated servers. Sites actively using these namespaces are recommended to secure them with DNSSEC (RFC 4035) by publishing and using trust anchors, which protects clients from accidentally importing unsigned responses from the Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: At first, a few computers might get a surprise 'no such name'. And places that care about being sure of answers should add DNSSEC, a way to check answers are genuine.
